title: Telling a story well
cando: tell a story with the background, the events in order and how people reacted

about.text: In this lesson you learn to tell a story well: you set the scene, tell the events in order and say how people reacted. You read a worker's account of an accident and the incident report about it. Then you tell a friend about a day you will never forget, and write it up as a short report.
goals: Set the scene of a story: It was getting dark, and people were going home.
Tell the events in order, and say what had happened before: Somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.
Say how people reacted: She screamed. We were all shocked.
Read an account and an incident report, and write the opening of a story.
Tell a memorable story to a friend, then write it up as a short report.

chapters.title: Four minutes in the yard
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you learn to tell a story well.
First, you listen to Tomasz. He works in the delivery yard of a big shop. Yesterday there was an accident at work, and today he tells his friend Amina about it.
Listen to how he starts. He doesn't start with the accident. He starts with the scene: It was getting dark, and most people were going home.
Then the event arrives: All of a sudden, we heard a loud noise.
And at the end, he tells her how it finished: In the end, the manager came and calmed everyone down.
Listen to Amina, too. A good listener reacts: Oh no! And then? Was anybody hurt?

chapters.title: Three past tenses in one story
chapters.text:
A good story uses three past tenses together.
The past continuous sets the scene. It was getting dark. People were going home. These things were already happening when the story started.
The past simple tells the events, one after another. We heard a noise. The trolley hit the shelves. Two shelves collapsed.
We often join the two with when. I was checking the shelves when we heard a noise. The long action is the background. The short action cuts across it.
The past perfect goes one step further back. It tells you what had happened before the story started. Somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.
When we speak, had is short and quiet. I'd forgotten. She'd gone home.
But don't use the past perfect for every event. When things happen in order, the past simple is enough: I got up, had a shower and left.

chapters.title: An account and a report
chapters.text:
Next, you read two texts about the same accident.
The first is Kwame's account for the staff newsletter. He writes it like a story. He tells you about the dark yard, the strange noise and how people felt.
The second is the incident report. It gives only the facts: the date, the time, the location, what took place and what was done.
Notice the difference. A story makes the reader feel something. A report helps the reader check what happened.
Then you write the opening of a story. Set the scene first: where it takes place, when, and what was happening. Then write the moment when everything changes.

chapters.title: Tell it, then write it up
chapters.text:
In the task, you tell a friend about a day you will never forget. It can be real, or you can invent it.
Start with the scene. Then tell the events in order. Say how people reacted, and how it ended.
Your friend reacts and asks questions: Oh no! What happened next?
Then you write the same story as a short report. This time, no feelings. Just the facts, in order: when, where, what happened, and what was done.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story from the Library. Before you read, look at the title and guess where it takes place.
Read it once for the plot: what happens, and to whom. Then read it again and notice how the writer sets the scene.

warmup.prompt: Think of a story you like to tell your friends. What kind of story is it?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. People love all kinds of stories. What makes a story good is how you tell it: the scene, the events in order, and how people reacted.

conversation.title: Four minutes in the yard
conversation.setting: Tomasz works in the delivery yard of a big shop. The day after an accident at work, he meets his friend Amina for a coffee.
lines: You look tired, Tomasz. Is everything all right?
Not really. Something happened at work yesterday, and I can't stop thinking about it.
Well, it was getting dark, and most people were going home. There was a strange atmosphere in the yard. Nobody was talking.
Kwame and I were checking the shelves when, all of a sudden, we heard a loud noise. A heavy trolley was rolling towards us.
Yes! Kwame shouted, and we jumped out of the way just in time. The trolley crashed into the shelves, and two of them collapsed.
No, luckily nobody was injured. But one of the drivers screamed. She was terrified. She thought somebody was under the boxes.
I'm not surprised. I'd be shocked too.
For a few seconds there was complete silence. We all held our breath. Then everyone rushed over to help.
So what happened in the end?
In the end, the manager came and calmed everyone down. It turned out that somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.

questions.q: What were Tomasz and Kwame doing when they heard the noise?
questions.why: Tomasz says: Kwame and I were checking the shelves when we heard a loud noise.

questions.q: How did one of the drivers react?
questions.why: Tomasz says: One of the drivers screamed, because she thought somebody was under the boxes.

questions.a: Somebody had left it at the top of the yard.
wrong: Kwame had pushed it by mistake.
questions.why: Tomasz says: It turned out that somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.

phrases.use: Setting the scene at the start of a story.
Bringing in the event that changes everything.
Asking the storyteller to go on.
Asking about injuries after an accident.
Saying what you found out later.
Showing that you understand how someone felt.

items.meaning: To move or do something very quickly, because there is no time to lose.
items.example: When the shelves came down, everyone rushed over to help.

items.meaning: To give a loud, high cry because you are afraid, hurt or very excited.
items.example: One of the drivers screamed when she saw the boxes fall.

items.meaning: To hit your foot against something, so that you almost fall or you fall.
items.example: I tripped over a cable in the dark.

items.meaning: To hit something by accident, so that it falls to the ground.
items.example: The trolley knocked over a pile of boxes.

items.meaning: To fall down suddenly, because it is broken or weak. A person can do this too, when they are very ill.
items.example: Two of the shelves collapsed under the weight.

items.meaning: Very surprised and upset, because something bad has happened.
items.example: We were all shocked when we heard the news.

items.meaning: Extremely frightened.
items.example: She was terrified that someone was under the boxes.

items.meaning: Hurt in an accident, or in a fight.
items.example: Luckily, nobody was injured.

items.meaning: A time when there is no sound at all.
items.example: For a few seconds, there was complete silence.

items.meaning: A place or a time with no light.
items.example: We waited in the darkness for the lights to come back on.

items.meaning: The feeling that a place or a situation gives you.
items.example: There was a strange atmosphere in the yard that evening.

items.meaning: Very quickly, at a moment when nobody expects it.
items.example: All of a sudden, the lights went out.

items.meaning: At the last possible moment, before it is too late.
items.example: We jumped out of the way just in time.

items.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment, because you are afraid or you are waiting to see what happens.
items.example: We all held our breath and waited.

items.meaning: To become less upset or excited, or to help another person feel less upset.
items.example: The manager asked everyone to calm down and move away from the shelves.

sound.title: Short was and were
sound.explain: In the past continuous, was and were are short and quiet, and the main verb is strong. Say I wz CHECKing, not I WAS checking. Listen to each group, then say it.
groups: I was checking · it was getting dark · she was waiting
we were talking · they were leaving · people were going home
lines: It was getting dark, and most people were going home.
Kwame and I were checking the shelves.
A heavy trolley was rolling towards us.

sayIt.instructions: Say Tomasz's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Did you set the scene slowly, and say the event with more energy?
lines: Well, it was getting dark, and most people were going home. There was a strange atmosphere in the yard. Nobody was talking.
Kwame and I were checking the shelves when, all of a sudden, we heard a loud noise. A heavy trolley was rolling towards us.
For a few seconds there was complete silence. We all held our breath. Then everyone rushed over to help.
In the end, the manager came and calmed everyone down. It turned out that somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Each one tells a different part of the story.
examples: It was getting dark, and most people were going home.
Kwame and I were checking the shelves when, all of a sudden, we heard a loud noise.
The trolley crashed into the shelves, and two of them collapsed.
Somebody had left the trolley at the top of the yard.
spot.question: Which verbs set the scene? Which verbs tell the events? Which action happened before everything else in the story?
spot.answer: Was getting, were going and were checking set the scene: they are in the past continuous. Heard, crashed and collapsed tell the events, one after another: they are in the past simple. Had left happened before all of it: it is in the past perfect.

rules.title: Setting the scene: I was checking the shelves when …
rule: Past continuous for the background: It was getting dark. People were going home.
Past simple for the events, in order: The trolley hit the shelves, and they collapsed.
when + past simple for an event that cuts across the background: We were checking the shelves when we heard a noise.
while + past continuous: While we were talking, the lights went out.
Start with the scene, then the event: It was raining, and nobody was around. Then I heard a scream.
rules.mistake: Not: I checked the shelves when a trolley was crashing into them. Say: I was checking the shelves when a trolley crashed into them.

rules.title: One step further back: the past perfect
rule: had + past participle: had left, had gone, had forgotten. It is the same for I, you, she and they.
It shows what happened before the main story: When we got there, the manager had already closed the area.
Short forms: I'd, she'd, we'd. Negative: hadn't. Nobody had put the brake on.
It often explains a cause: She was upset because somebody had taken her seat.
Events in order don't need it: I got up, had a shower and left.
rules.mistake: Not: When I arrived, the meeting already started. Say: When I arrived, the meeting had already started.

practice.q: I ___ the shelves when the lights went out.
practice.why: The background action takes the past continuous, and I goes with was.

practice.q: While we ___ lunch, the fire alarm went off.
We were waiting at the bus stop when a car ___ into a lamp post.
practice.why: A short, sudden event that cuts across the background takes the past simple.

practice.q: When I got to the station, my train ___ .
practice.why: The train left before I got there, so we use the past perfect.

practice.q: She couldn't open the door because she ___ her keys at home.
practice.why: She left the keys at home before she tried the door, so we use the past perfect.

practice.q: It was dark, and I ___ over a bag on the floor.
practice.why: A short event in the story takes the past simple.

practice.q: By the time the manager arrived, we ___ the area.
practice.why: We cleared the area before the manager arrived, so we use the past perfect.

practice.q: What ___ you doing when the accident happened?
practice.why: What were you doing? asks about the background.

practice.q: I got up, ___ a quick shower and left for work.
practice.why: These events happen in order, so the past simple is enough.

practice.q: I didn't recognise Omar at first because he ___ his beard.
practice.why: He shaved off his beard before I saw him, so we use the past perfect.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a moment when something surprising happened to you: at work, on a journey or at home. Write the first four sentences of the story. Set the scene with the past continuous, bring in the event with the past simple, and use the past perfect once.
yourTurn.model: It was a cold Friday evening, and the office was almost empty. I was finishing a report, and my colleague Mei was talking on the phone. All of a sudden, the fire alarm went off. Nobody had told us about a fire drill, so we were quite worried.

text.title: Four minutes in the yard, and the incident report
text.body:
FOUR MINUTES IN THE YARD
An account by Kwame Mensah, yard team

It was a Tuesday evening in November, and it was getting dark. The last lorry had left, and the yard was almost empty. Tomasz and I were checking the shelves at the north end. Nobody was talking.
Then we heard a mysterious noise behind us, like thunder a long way off. I turned round. A heavy trolley was rolling down the slope towards us, faster and faster. I shouted, and we jumped out of the way just in time. The trolley crashed into the end of the shelves, and two of them came down.
For a moment, nobody moved. Then Lena, one of our drivers, screamed. She thought somebody was under the boxes. Luckily, nobody was.
The following day, we found out what had happened. Somebody had left the trolley at the top of the slope, and nobody had put the brake on. The whole thing took four minutes, but I will remember it for years.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE FORM: this company does not exist.
WENDLOW HOME SUPPLIES · INCIDENT REPORT
Reference: IN-4471
Location: delivery yard, north end
Date and time: Tuesday 14 November, 17:04
Reported by: K. Mensah, yard team
What took place: A trolley rolled down the slope and hit the end of the shelves. Two shelves collapsed.
Injuries: none. Nobody was standing next to the shelves.
Cause: The trolley had been left at the top of the slope without the brake on.
Action: The area was closed at 17:10. All trolleys were checked the following day.
Witnesses: T. Nowak, L. Fischer

gist.q: What are the two texts about?
gist.a: the same accident, told in two different ways
wrong: two different accidents in the yard
a safety course for the yard team
gist.why: Kwame tells the story of the accident, and the report gives the facts about the same accident.

gist.q: Which text tells you how people felt?
gist.why: Only the account says how people reacted, for example that Lena screamed.

detail.q: Where did the accident take place?
detail.a: at the north end of the delivery yard
detail.why: The report says: Location: delivery yard, north end.

detail.a: She thought somebody was under the boxes.
detail.why: Kwame writes: She thought somebody was under the boxes.

detail.q: Why did the trolley roll down the slope?
detail.a: Nobody had put the brake on.
wrong: The shelves had fallen on it.
detail.why: Both texts say the trolley was left at the top of the slope without the brake on.

detail.q: When were all the trolleys checked?
detail.why: The report says: All trolleys were checked the following day.

items.meaning: A description of what happened, told or written by one person.
items.example: Kwame wrote an account of the accident for the staff newsletter.

items.meaning: The place where something is, or where something happens.
items.example: Write the exact location of the accident on the form.

items.meaning: To happen, usually at a known time and place.
items.example: The accident took place at about five o'clock.

items.meaning: The part of a car, a bike or a trolley that makes it slow down or stop.
items.example: Always put the brake on before you leave the van.

items.meaning: Ground that goes up or down, like the side of a hill.
items.example: The trolley rolled down the slope towards us.

items.meaning: A person in a story, a film or a play.
items.example: The main character is a young nurse on her first night at work.

items.meaning: What happens in a story, from the beginning to the end.
items.example: I can't remember the plot, but I loved the film.

items.meaning: The first part of a story, a film or a speech.
items.example: A good opening makes you want to read on.

items.meaning: Strange, and hard to understand or explain.
items.example: We heard a mysterious noise behind the door.

items.meaning: The next day, after the day you are talking about.
items.example: The following day, the manager checked every trolley in the yard.

items.meaning: To write something quickly, so that you don't forget it.
items.example: I noted down the time of the accident on my phone.

model.title: The opening of a story
model.body:
THE LAST TRAIN
It was nearly midnight, and the last train was running late. Rain was falling on the empty platform, and a cold wind was blowing through the station. I was sitting on a bench, reading, when all of a sudden the lights went out.
In the darkness, I heard footsteps. Somebody was walking slowly towards me. I held my breath.
Then a voice said my name, very quietly. That was strange, because I hadn't told anyone that I was coming home that night.

write.task: Write the opening of a story, true or invented, in 60 to 100 words. Set the scene first: where and when it takes place, and what was happening. Then write the moment when everything changes. Try to end with something mysterious, so that the reader wants to know what happens next.
checklist: I said where and when the story takes place.
I set the scene with two or more verbs in the past continuous: was raining, were talking.
I told the event that changes everything in the past simple.
I used the past perfect once, for something that had happened earlier.

card.title: A day I will never forget
card.situation: A friend asks you about a day you will never forget: an accident, a lucky escape, a strange evening or a funny mistake. It can be real, or you can invent it. Later, somebody asks you for a short written report about the same event: your manager, your landlord or the building manager.
card.goal: Tell the story so that your friend can see the scene and follow the events. Then write a short report of the same event, with only the facts, in order.

phrases: You'll never guess what happened to me last week.
It was about seven in the evening, and I was …
Everybody was shocked. Nobody knew what to do.
It turned out that somebody had …
prepare.notes: Make notes before you speak. The scene: where, when, and what was happening. Three events, in order. How people reacted. How it ended. Then note down the facts for the report: the date, the time, the location, what took place and what was done.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, tell your story to a partner in about two minutes. Your partner reacts and asks two questions. Then change roles. At the end, write the short report of your story, and your teacher checks the order of the facts.
doIt.wehel: You are my friend. I want to tell you about a day I will never forget. Listen, react and ask me questions: Where were you? What were you doing? What happened next? How did people react? How did it end? Then help me write a short report of the same event, with only the facts. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Stuck in the lift
lines: You'll never guess what happened to me on Thursday.
It was about seven in the evening, and I was working late. It was getting dark, and there was a storm outside.
Sounds like the opening of a film!
Wait! I got into the lift with a woman from the fourth floor. All of a sudden, the lights went out, and the lift stopped between two floors.
Oh no! What did you do?
She screamed. She was terrified. For a minute there was total darkness and silence. I held my breath.
Then I found the alarm button and pressed it. I told her an engineer was coming, and she calmed down a bit.
How long were you in there?
Forty minutes! In the end, an engineer opened the doors. It turned out that the storm had cut the power to the whole building.
No, nobody was injured. The following day, I wrote a short report for the building manager.
compare: Did you set the scene first: the time, the place and what was happening?
Did you tell the events in order, with All of a sudden, Then and In the end?
Did you say how people reacted: shocked, terrified, calm?
In your report, did you give only the facts: the date, the time, the location, what took place and what was done?

canDo: I can set the scene of a story with the past continuous.
I can tell the events of a story in order, and say how people reacted.
I can use the past perfect for something that had happened earlier.
I can read an account and an incident report and find the facts.
I can write the opening of a story, and a short report of an event.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Where and when does the story take place? What do you think will happen?
reading.talk: Which moment in the story was the most exciting? How did the characters react? Tell the story to Wehel in five sentences: the scene, three events and the ending.

quiz.q: I ___ dinner when the phone rang.
quiz.why: The background action takes the past continuous: I was cooking.

quiz.q: When we got to the cinema, the film ___ .
quiz.why: The film started before we got there, so we use the past perfect.

quiz.q: It was dark, and I ___ over a box in the corridor.
quiz.why: You trip over something when your foot hits it and you almost fall.

quiz.q: Everybody was very frightened. They were ___ .
Nobody said a word. There was complete ___ .
quiz.why: Silence is a time with no sound at all.

quiz.q: The van rolled down the hill because nobody had put the ___ on.
quiz.why: A brake stops a vehicle; a break is a rest from work.

quiz.q: When I was a child, I ___ play football in the street every evening.
quiz.why: Used to + verb talks about a past habit.
Since 2019 means up to now, so we use the present perfect.

quiz.q: That's the colleague ___ car was stolen last week.
quiz.why: Whose shows that something belongs to a person: her car.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the yard conversation in pairs, one learner as Tomasz and one as Amina. Then each learner gives a one-sentence scene (It was getting dark when…), and the others react: Oh no! And then?

Day 2: a chain story. Learners take turns to add one sentence, changing between background (past continuous) and events (past simple). The last learner explains the story with the past perfect: It turned out that…
Day 3: the task. Learners tell a memorable story to a partner in two minutes, and the partner asks questions. Then each pair writes a short report of one story. Check the order of the facts together.
Day 4: talk about the book: the characters, the plot and the most exciting moment. Two learners read their story openings aloud, and the class chooses the most mysterious one.
